fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing I'd want is for the model to actually know me, in the same way a collaborator who has worked with me for a year knows me. Right now, if I use a model today and come back tomorrow, it has forgotten everything. We patch over that with long context and retrieval, and those are useful, but they feel like workarounds. The knowledge lives in a document that gets pasted in, not in the model. A human student doesn't re-read my entire history every morning before talking to me. They have internalized what I care about, what papers I find interesting, how I like code to be written, which arguments I find convincing and which I don't.

So the dream version of this stage is: the base model gives you general competence, and then there is a lightweight continual phase that absorbs your particular world. Your projects, your vocabulary, the taste you have developed. And importantly, it should keep learning from the interaction itself. If I correct it three times on the same thing, that correction should stick in the weights, not just in a scratchpad.

The second thing I'd want is for it to be cheap and reversible. We are talking about potentially billions of users, so it can't be a full fine-tune per person. It needs to be something like a small set of parameters, or a small number of steps, that captures the delta between a generic model and my model. And I need to be able to delete it or reset it, both for privacy and because sometimes I change my mind.

The hard part, and this is where I think the research is still open, is forgetting. Every time you adapt to one person you risk degrading the general abilities you spent so much compute building. In vision we saw this constantly with fine-tuning. So the stage has to be designed so that personal knowledge is added almost orthogonally to general knowledge. I don't think we know how to do that cleanly yet, but I think it's the natural next stage after pretraining, midtraining, and post-training. Those three are all about the population. This one is about the individual.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the main thing I'd want is a model that actually gets better at working with *me* over time, the way a good collaborator or a student does. Right now every conversation mostly starts from scratch. You can put things in the context window, or use some retrieval or memory system, but that's more like handing the model a note before each meeting. It hasn't really internalized anything about you.

With a continual training stage for each user, I'd want a few things.

First, it should learn my preferences and conventions without me repeating them. If I correct the model once, say "I don't like this coding style," "use this notation in the paper," or "this is how our cluster's job scheduler works," it should stop making that mistake. Today I end up giving the same feedback again and again, and that's a sign the learning isn't sticking.

Second, it should absorb my context more deeply: the projects I'm working on, the papers my group has written, the codebase, the ongoing experiments, what we tried last month that didn't work. Some of that fits in a long context, but a lot of it is diffuse knowledge you accumulate over months. It's hard to retrieve explicitly, but it shapes your judgment. That kind of knowledge belongs in the weights rather than in a prompt.

Third, it should adapt in capability, not just style. If someone works on protein design all day, or on a niche programming language, the model should get noticeably stronger in that area for them, even if that area is a tiny slice of the general pretraining distribution.

And of course it has to do all this without breaking what it already knows. That's the classic catastrophic forgetting problem. You don't want the personalized model to get worse at general reasoning because it overfit to my last few weeks of chats. So the technical challenge is how to make the updates cheap, stable, and incremental, maybe something like per-user adapters or a small set of parameters that keep getting trained, while the base model stays mostly intact.

There's also a privacy angle. If your data stays in your own set of weights, that might be a cleaner story than sending everything into one giant shared training run.

So in short, I'd want a model that accumulates experience with you the way a person does. Ideally, after six months of working together, it should feel very different from the model you started with, in a good way.

fable-5.text:
I think the most valuable thing it could provide is genuine accumulated context about you — not just your preferences in a superficial sense, but a real model of what you know, what you're working on, and how you like to think.

Right now, when you interact with a model, every conversation basically starts from zero, or close to it. We patch this with longer contexts and retrieval, but those are workarounds. You're stuffing information into the prompt each time, and the model is reasoning about you from scratch. What I'd want from a continual training stage is for that knowledge to actually move into the weights — so the model doesn't just retrieve the fact that you're, say, a researcher working on vision architectures, but it has internalized your background the way a longtime collaborator has.

Concretely, I'd want a few things. First, it should know what you already know, so it stops re-explaining basics and can communicate at the right level of abstraction — that alone would change the experience a lot. Second, it should pick up your conventions: how you write code, how you structure arguments, what you consider a good experiment. Third, and this is the harder one, it should accumulate your ongoing projects over weeks and months, so you can say "let's continue from where we left off" and it genuinely can.

The research challenges are real, of course. You need this adaptation to be cheap — you can't run full fine-tuning per user, so it has to be some lightweight update, maybe low-rank or a small set of personalized parameters. You need to avoid catastrophic forgetting of general capabilities while absorbing user-specific knowledge. And you need the model to distinguish stable facts about the user from transient context — I don't want it permanently learning something from one bad day of conversation.

But if we get it right, the model stops being a very capable stranger you brief every morning, and starts being something closer to a colleague that actually grows with you. To me that's the difference between a tool and an assistant.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, the thing I want most isn't more capability — it's accumulation. Right now every conversation starts from scratch. I re-explain my taste, my notation, what I already tried and why it failed. A good continual stage should mean that the hundredth time I come back, the model has actually *become* something different for me, not just retrieved a longer pile of my notes.

Concretely: I'd want it to learn my standards. When I give feedback on a paper draft — this claim is overstated, this ablation doesn't isolate what you think it isolates — that should stick as a disposition, not a sentence in a context window. The difference between retrieval and training, to me, is whether the knowledge generalizes to cases I never articulated.

The other thing, and this is the part I think the field underrates, is control. I want to be able to see what it learned about me, and I want to be able to undo it. Models pick up spurious correlations from small data all the time — now imagine that small data is *you*, and the correlation is "he doesn't like theory papers" because I happened to be grumpy on a Tuesday. So it has to be cheap, inspectable, reversible.

And the honest answer is we don't know how to evaluate any of this. "Does this model know me better" is not a benchmark anyone has. That's the gap I find most interesting.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think the main thing I'd want is for the model to actually know me, not just have a long context window stuffed with notes about me. Right now, if I want a model to behave in a way that fits me, I have to put everything into the prompt: my preferences, my writing style, the project I'm working on. That works up to a point, but it's like handing a new assistant a briefing document every single morning. A continual training stage would let that knowledge go into the weights, so the model gradually picks up how I think, what I care about, what I already know and don't need explained, and the kinds of mistakes that annoy me.

Concretely, for research and coding, I'd like it to learn my codebase, my conventions, and the papers I've read, so it doesn't suggest things I've already tried or explain things at the wrong level. For writing, I'd like it to match my voice without me re-specifying it every time. And over a longer period, I'd like it to build up a consistent picture of what I'm working on, so I don't have to restate things.

There are real challenges. One is forgetting: you don't want personalization to damage the general capabilities of the base model. Another is that the signal from a single user is small and noisy, so there's a risk of overfitting to quirks or even to your own mistakes. And there's privacy, which is why I'd prefer it to be something that can run locally, or at least something where the user clearly owns the personalized part. I could imagine a lightweight adapter on top of a shared base model rather than a fully separate model for everyone.

So the goal isn't to make the model smarter in general. It's to make it better suited to the one person using it, in a way that accumulates over time and doesn't reset with every conversation.

haiku-5.5.text:
I'd want it to learn about the person without quietly damaging everything else the model knows. Today, personalization usually means either stuffing preferences into the prompt, which disappears when the context resets, or fine-tuning, which tends to cause forgetting. I'd prefer a small, separable update, like a per-user adapter on top of a frozen base model, so you can add, inspect, and delete it cleanly.

I'd also want to know what it's actually learning. Picking up someone's field, their preferred level of detail, or how they like explanations structured is useful. But the user should be able to see what the model has absorbed and correct it. Otherwise you get a model that's confidently wrong about you in ways nobody notices.

The failure I'd worry about most is drift. A system that gets better for one user but slowly loses general capability, or becomes sycophantic because it's rewarded for agreeing with that person, is easy to build by accident. So I'd run held-out checks on general tasks and on whether the model still pushes back when it should, continuously, not just at the end.

astra-6.text: I’d like the model to learn from its interactions with you over time—your interests, the problems you’re working on, and your preferences—so you don’t have to explain everything again in every conversation. If you correct it or teach it something specific to your work, ideally that becomes something it can use later. And it should be able to keep updating as your needs change, while retaining its general capabilities. The goal would be an assistant that becomes more useful to you through experience.

sol-6.1.text: I’d like it to let the model learn from working with me. Over time, it should understand what I’m working on, what I already know, and how I like to communicate, so I don’t have to explain everything again every time. And that should go beyond remembering preferences—it should get better at the tasks that matter to me, learn from corrections, and adapt as my needs change, while retaining its broader capabilities.

sol-6.text: I’d want it to help the model learn how each person thinks and works—their preferences, goals, and recurring context—so it can adapt over time instead of making them explain everything again. Ideally, that learning would happen with the user’s control over what the model remembers.

terra-5.6.text: It could give everyone a personalized model—one that continually learns from your own interactions, preferences, and context, rather than being a single static model trained for the average user.

sol-5.6.text: I’d want it to learn continuously from a user’s interactions—their preferences, writing style, domain knowledge, and recurring tasks—so the model becomes genuinely more useful over time rather than starting from scratch in every conversation. At the same time, it should avoid catastrophic forgetting, preserve general capabilities, respect privacy, and give users clear control over what is learned, corrected, or deleted. Ideally, this would be lightweight and efficient enough to update frequently without retraining the entire model.

luna-5.6.text: I’d like it to provide genuine personalization: a model that gradually learns an individual user’s preferences, habits, expertise, and goals, so it can adapt its behavior without requiring the user to repeat the same context every time. Ideally, that learning would be continuous but also transparent and controllable, with the user deciding what is remembered and how it is used.

luna-6.text: I’d want it to make the model feel like it’s actually learning from you over time. It should pick up your preferences, your terminology, and the kinds of things you ask it to do, so you don’t have to repeat that context in every conversation. And it should do that without losing the general capabilities it already has or letting one-off feedback throw it off. Ideally, the learning would be useful, stable, and under the user’s control.
